trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.title: Wayfarer's Guide, Mk I
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.blurb: Everything you need to start reading the ground.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page1.title: Ground that remembers
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page1.body: Walk the same line often enough and the ground gives way to it. That is the whole of this mod: grass thins to earth, earth packs down and sinks, sand and gravel scuff, stone cracks and goes dull. Nothing is placed and nothing is destroyed - the world keeps a quiet note of how often each square has been crossed, and draws the ground accordingly. Stop using a route and it recovers on its own.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page2.title: How a path forms
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page2.body: Every crossing of a square counts, unless snow is lying on it: a layer of snow takes the traffic in the ground's place and is trodden through first, one layer at a time, because a path across a snowfield wears the snow away before it wears anything underneath - so a square under snow takes no wear at all until the last of the snow over it has gone. Enough crossings advance it one gradation, and enough gradations carry it into the next surface along its chain: grass into the earth it was growing out of, a stone road into the cobble it breaks up as, then into the grit that came off it, then into the ground it was laid on. Every one of them ends in a rut that visibly sinks below its neighbours, and unless the server has switched it off, a square worn a whole further threshold past even that is simply gone - it drops nothing, because what wore away was carried off a grain at a time by whatever walked over it. The run is the same length whatever it passes through, and each step costs what the ground is made of rather than what the top of it currently looks like, so a road that has broken up is no quicker to finish off than one that has not. Different ground gives way at different rates: snow and sand mark almost at once, stone takes a very long time. Slabs and stairs count as the stuff they were cut from and wear on exactly the same terms, for exactly as much traffic and exactly as long a recovery - the rut is simply drawn half as deep on a slab, because half a block cannot lose eight pixels and still be there, and a stair shows its wear without sinking at all - a stair's drawn shape and the shape you stand on are one and the same, so a dip in the picture would be a dip the server has not got. Horses, carts and crowds count for more than a single walker. The plants standing in a route go down with the route. Not at the first scuff: a tuft of grass, a cane or a cactus comes down when the square it stands on physically drops a level, on the reasoning that by then there is nothing left under it. A stalk goes in full, because neither cane nor cactus will stand on nothing. Anything planted in hoed ground is left alone, and so is anything with roots worth keeping: a sapling or a flower holds its square at the end of the run that ground takes on the face it still has, so a path forming through an orchard darkens around the trees rather than felling them. The wear underneath goes on being counted the whole time - break the plant and the square catches up at once.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page3.title: How it heals
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page3.body: Ground nobody has walked on recovers by itself, a gradation at a time, over in-game days. It happens even in chunks nobody is standing in, so a route abandoned while you are away really will have grown back when you return. Bone meal hurries a patch along if you would rather not wait, and so will the tampers.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page4.title: The Tamper
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page4.body: A tamper shapes ground deliberately. Left-click wears one gradation in; sneak and left-click mends one back. Right-click mends a patch around where you point, paying in whatever the ground is made of - dirt for dirt, cobble for cobble, two blocks a patch by default. A patch that crosses two kinds of ground pays for each, and leaves alone whatever you are not carrying the material for. Mending you pay for earns a little experience; mending that costs nothing earns none. Sneak and right-click pins a square so neither traffic nor time will move it. It is made in whatever metal your world has; harder metals last longer, and gold trades durability for reach.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page5.title: The Chunk Tamper
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page5.body: The same gestures over a whole cube instead of a square. Right-click air to resize it, sneak and right-click air to change how many gradations one use moves. Every gradation it puts back is paid for - a block of that ground, or of whatever its family accepts in its place, for every four, by default - so it costs as much as it puts back, and each kind of ground in the cube pays its own. It is built from a tamper of its own metal ringed in more of that metal, so a diamond one needs a diamond tamper. Ctrl and right-click opens its settings screen.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page6.title: The Wayfarer's Tamper
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page6.body: The last rung of the ladder. It works any ground for nothing, never wears out, and is built around a chunk tamper with a nether star set above it: a netherite chunk tamper where the pack can make one and its harder, GregTech-tuned recipes are switched on, a diamond one otherwise, and where no diamond one can be made either, the longest-lasting chunk tamper the pack can make. It also does everything the others do a little better - it reinforces a block straight to whatever level you choose for a single material, where a plain chunk tamper must climb one at a time.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page7.title: Reading the ground
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page7.body: Look at a worn square with WAILA and it will tell you how far along it is, how long since anything crossed it, and when it will recover. Reinforcement, spawn wards and a lit square's color show there too. If you use JourneyMap, worn ground is drawn in a color that has travelled toward whatever that ground is turning into - a turf path leaves green and arrives at earth in step with how far along its run it has walked - and darkened by how heavily it has been used, so a road on the map reads as a road rather than only as a material; a square that has only just started to go is therefore still mostly the color it began as, because the point is to show how far along a route is and not merely that something has happened to it. Any other map is only ever told what material a square is, since the per-position color is handed to JourneyMap and to nothing else: the vanilla map item in particular works from a fixed palette with no darker sibling to pick, so it is given the right material - earth once the turf has gone - and nothing about how worn that square is. With a shader pack running, worn ground keeps the material the block underneath it had, and gives it up only as it wears through into something else - so a stone road stops shining as it breaks into cobble rather than the moment anybody walks on it. Worn ground also keeps what the block underneath it was doing: anything that glowed goes on glowing, anything that scattered spores or sparks goes on scattering them, and worn ice is still ice underfoot.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page8.title: If you would rather not
trmtgtnh.guide.mk1.page8.body: Every part of this is optional, with one exception, and it is the shipped default rather than an edge. One client setting hides worn ground for you alone without affecting anyone else or stopping the server tracking it, so switching it back on brings every path straight back - except where the ruts are real enough to walk down into, which is what physicalDecay under general asks for out of the box. There the drawing is held on whatever the world is running, in a world of your own as much as on somebody else's, because a hollow you can fall into and cannot see is worse than one you did not want to look at; a world whose physicalDecay is set to visual or to off hands the choice straight back. On a server the operator can turn wear off entirely, exclude blocks or whole dimensions, and set how fast anything gives way. No wear is ever written into the world and no block of this mod's own is ever placed in it, so removing the mod leaves nothing behind that a world would not know. Three things it ships doing are exceptions and say so in their own settings: ground worn all the way through is removed, a plant standing on a square that sinks is knocked loose, and a layer of snow trodden all the way through is taken away. All three destroy real blocks, and none of them is undone by taking the mod out again.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.title: Wayfarer's Guide, Mk II
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.blurb: The numbers, the storage, and every knob there is.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page1.title: Families and chains
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page1.body: Every surface the mod knows belongs to a family - grass, dirt, sand, gravel, cobble, stone, snow, ice, nether, end. A family has a chain: the run of appearances it passes through from pristine to fully worn, and how far it sinks on the way. Grass runs into bare earth and then into a rut; stone stays stone and simply cracks. Detection is by block, so a modded turf joins the grass family and wears in its own colors.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page2.title: Where wear lives
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page2.body: No eroded block is ever written into the world. Each worn position is one small record - family, gradation, depth, progress, and the world-time it was last touched - packed into a chunk's own saved data. That is why the mod can be removed without leaving unknown blocks behind, and why one player can hide the whole thing without the server or anyone else noticing.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page3.title: Thresholds and speed
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page3.body: Each gradation has a threshold drawn at random between the family's minimum and maximum, which is what stops a path from advancing in perfectly straight bands. The speed multiplier is applied when the threshold is compared rather than when it is drawn, so changing it takes effect on ground that already exists instead of only on ground made afterwards.|That draw is not the whole price. Each family also carries a cost curve, and the curve multiplies the draw by where along its run the gradation sits, so on most surfaces the first gradation and the last cost nothing like the same traffic. Every step costing the same is not what any of these surfaces do, and it was the reason early wear read as inert: the gradation you actually watch appear, the first, cost exactly as much as the last.|flat holds one price the whole way, and is what stone, cobble, netherrack and end stone are given - dressed stone does not compact underfoot, and the hundredth scuff costs what the first did. sod, for grass and dirt, starts cheap and ends about four fifths dearer, because turf tears at a touch and the earth beneath it is packed and rooted and does not. settle, for sand and gravel, climbs to two and a half times, because loose grains and loose stones displace under the first passes and then settle into a shape they have already found. pack, for snow, climbs fourfold and stops climbing three quarters of the way along, because once snow is thoroughly packed there is nothing left to compress. glaze, for ice, climbs twelvefold in a straight line and never levels off at all, because scuffing ice does not compact it but merely polishes what is left.|Whichever curve a family is given, the total does not move. The multipliers over a whole run average to exactly one, so a curve only redistributes what the run costs and can never quietly make a family easier or harder while appearing to be a change of shape. What changes is where the cost sits: how quickly a path first shows, against how hard it is to drive one all the way down. It does mean the traffic charged for a single gradation can sit well outside the family's own minimum and maximum - ice is drawn between ten and sixteen, and its first gradation is charged nearer two.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page4.title: Healing
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page4.body: Recovery is measured in in-game days per gradation, per family, and it is worked out from absolute world time rather than by ticking. The difference between the stored last-touched time and the clock at load says exactly how much recovery a chunk missed while it was unloaded, so it catches up in one pass. A server switched off for a week heals nothing, because no in-game time passed - and by default neither does one left running with nobody on it, so a golem tending a road overnight keeps what it did.|How long a gradation takes is that family's own figure, written in the column beside its thresholds and nowhere derived. It used to be worked out from what the family cost to wear - one constant times its average threshold - which held the whole table together from a single number and made it lie, because snow and sand cost almost exactly the same traffic to mark and recover nothing like alike: fresh snow covers a track in under a week, and a rut in sand wants the better part of a month of wind. So each family now owns its recovery outright, and the wear table sets the two columns side by side for every family, which is the place to look after changing either. A fully worn path left entirely alone takes six in-game days to disappear on snow, thirty on sand, thirty-one on ice, forty-five on gravel, a hundred on dirt, a hundred and twenty-five on turf, a hundred and seventy on cobble, three hundred and twenty on stone, and four hundred in the Nether or the End, where there is no weather to fill anything in. What each pair of numbers really says is how much traffic it takes to hold ground where it is, and that runs from about seven and a half crossings an in-game day for gravel to sixteen for stone - and to more for the two that mend in days rather than months, thirty-two for snow and forty for ice.|Rain shortens four of those while it is actually falling on the square in question: turf, earth, sand and gravel mend at twice their rate in the wet, because a downpour on a dirt track is the closest thing this game has to the real mechanism. Nothing else takes the discount, since rain does not mend dressed stone. It is a discount and never a gate - sheltered ground mends at the ordinary rate rather than not at all. Making a family wait for weather instead of merely being helped by it is a separate setting under weather, and it is off out of the box.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page5.title: The wear textures
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page5.body: Nothing is shipped pre-drawn. When the atlas is stitched, each surface's wear is generated from that block's own pixels, so a modded dirt wears in its own color and a resource pack retextures worn ground for free. How many pictures each run gets, how many pattern variations, and how many blocks get their own set rather than a family stand-in are all settings under client and surfaces.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page6.title: Wear patterns
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page6.body: Each family names how it should be drawn wearing, and there are eleven. Grass takes the cover off in patches and lets the face underneath show through, which is what turf does and what anything with a different underside does.|Crack splits a surface along a generated fracture network that widens and branches as it wears. Smooth flattens it toward its own average and darkens it, for something that buffs shiny underfoot. Dirt rubs a growing patch of it away, which is what a trodden path is, and is what anything the setting does not recognise falls back to - the older sand and polish names among them, so no config file breaks.|Four more are those same looks with a different hand on them. Cracked lite, rubbed away lite and cracked rubbed lite stop about halfway along the run their full versions finish, so a face grimes and hairlines without ever breaking up and a path stays a scuff. Every picture a lite look draws is one its full version genuinely passes through, which is why they are the same thing shown twice rather than two things. Smoothed heavy goes the other way and takes rather more of the relief with it, leaving about a third of the light and dark the block began with.|The last three do two things in one look, and the name says which order. Smoothed cracked and smoothed rubbed buff the whole face flat first and then crack it or wear a track across part of it, because everything the second half aims at is read out of the surface it is handed, and buffing afterwards would only close up the very fissures and the very track that had just been made. Cracked rubbed goes the other way round, and for a measured reason rather than a preference: cracking last blurs a track's edge away to a quarter of what it was, while a track worn last leaves the rest of the face carrying the fracture network exactly as a plain crack drew it.|Any family can be set to any of the eleven, and the wear table shows you what each one does to your own blocks before you choose.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page7.title: Tamper modes
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page7.body: An enchantment unlocks a mode on the two big tampers, and the settings screen cycles between the modes a tool actually carries. Reinforcing raises a block's blast resistance, three levels, the last fully blast-proof, and hardens it against feet as well: each level adds a whole extra lifetime of traffic, so a fully reinforced road takes four times the walking to wear. Warding bars hostile or passive mobs from spawning on a block. Wayfinding makes ground glow, in any of sixteen colors - click a lit square again to step the color on, left-click to step it back, sneak to put it out. Only worn ground can be lit, because the glow is emitted by the ghost the mod paints over it, so wear a path before lighting it. Each mode costs a material to apply and is shown in WAILA.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page8.title: The grace period
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page8.body: Break a block and everything the position carried - wear, reinforcement, ward - is set aside rather than dropped. Put the exact same block back in the same spot within the window and all of it returns. A different block placed meanwhile neither takes the record nor cancels it, so swapping a block out and back works. The window is fifteen real minutes by default and can be set to zero to forget immediately.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page9.title: Where the settings are
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page9.body: presets sits above everything else, because it is the shortest way to a whole opinion: five choosers, each an axis - quality, wear, healing, phases and depth - so that wanting slow wear and quick recovery is something to ask for rather than a compromise to work out. Each moves every family at once, and reads 'custom' when the numbers underneath it no longer match one of its rungs, so editing a number keeps the edit rather than having it overwritten.|general holds the rules of wear itself and belongs to the server. client is yours alone and survives visiting other worlds. families holds one heading per surface - its thresholds, how many days it takes to recover, its cost curve, its look, and how deep it sinks - and is where one family is retuned rather than all of them. surfaces decides what counts as what. multipliers says what each creature weighs. healing decides whether recovery happens at all, whether it pauses while nobody is connected, what mending pays in experience, and one rate laid over the top of the days each family owns - the days themselves live under families now, and are that family's own figure rather than anything worked out from what the surface cost to wear. trampling decides what a route does to the plants standing in it and to the leaves walked across it, and changes nothing about vanilla's own rule for trampling farmland. weather decides where rain and snow are counted as falling, both for a family set to mend only in the wet and for whether lying snow takes the traffic instead of the ground beneath it. performance holds the ceilings that keep all of this cheap, and changes only how much is watched at once, never how ground behaves.|explosions, impacts, reinforce, spawnward and pathlight each hold their own feature. golem holds the Golem of Ways, its upgrades and what it may reach into, and is where it is switched off entirely. potions holds the two draughts. loot decides whether this mod's tools and books turn up in the chests the world generates. spawnitems decides what a player is handed the first time they arrive in a world, and every entry in it ships off. integration holds what this mod writes for other mods that are present and never links against: the pack personality switch, and then separate switches for the quest chapter, for the trophy definitions, and for whether an operator is told that a world's questbook has not taken the chapter yet.|Six of those - golem, pathlight, spawnward, loot, spawnitems and integration - are not drawn on the in-game settings screen, which names what it shows by hand rather than walking the file. They are in the config file all the same, and a text editor is the way to reach them.
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page10.title: Compatibility
trmtgtnh.guide.mk2.page10.body: The mod runs on Forge or Fabric and needs nothing else. Where WAILA, a minimap, or a GregTech pack's own materials are present it uses them, and where they are not it does without. The renderer hooks are optional: if a future renderer moved one the cost is a cosmetic blemish, never a failure to start. Two hooks are not optional, and neither of them is a renderer hook. One puts a worn stair's real facing back where the stair rules read it, because a stair drawn and clicked with the wrong geometry is not a blemish. The other gives the server the collision shape of a rut it never dug, which is the whole of what general.physicalDecay=real rests on - ground drawn as a hollow that the server still holds at full height is a dip you can see and cannot step into.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.title: Wayfarer's Guide: Commands
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.blurb: Every command, every argument, with examples.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page1.title: /trmt
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page1.body: Everything lives under one command. Typed alone it prints its usage. Every subcommand but one needs operator permission, because most of them change the server's own settings or its stored wear. The one is version, which anybody may run: it says which build of the mod this is and which game and loader it is for, whether a newer one is out, and whether the mods it needs are new enough. Five of the others only report and change nothing - status, surfaces, here, golem and mapcolor - so they are safe to run at any time, but an operator still has to be the one running them.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page2.title: status
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page2.body: /trmt status - what the mod is doing right now: whether wear is enabled, how many chunks hold records, how many positions are tracked, and how many clients are subscribed to the overlay. The first thing to run when something looks wrong.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page3.title: enable, disable, purge
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page3.body: /trmt enable and /trmt disable turn wear on and off for the whole server. Disabling keeps every record, but healing runs on the world clock whether wear is on or off, so a long spell disabled reads as a long spell nobody walked. /trmt purge erases all stored wear in loaded chunks and cannot be undone - it is the one command worth thinking twice about.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page4.title: reload
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page4.body: /trmt reload re-reads the config from disk and applies what changed. Numbers take effect at once. Anything that changes how the wear textures are generated is rebuilt by whatever draws the world, by itself, and the command says so when that is the case.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page5.title: surfaces, here, mapcolor
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page5.body: /trmt surfaces [family] lists what the mod has detected as wearable, optionally narrowed to one family - the quickest way to find out why a block does or does not wear. /trmt here reports the record for the square you are standing on. /trmt mapcolor, asked by a player, gives the map color of the square you are standing on beside that of the ground one step east, which is where to look when a worn square is drawn the wrong color on a map.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page6.title: showcase
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page6.body: /trmt showcase [radius] wears the ground around you through its full range, so you can see every gradation at once without walking a path in. A quick way to judge a setting.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page7.title: demonstrate
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page7.body: /trmt demonstrate builds platforms in the air, one per surface the pack has, each worn from pristine to fully gone across its squares. Size is given as NxN or NxNxN, y=<h> sets the height, max=<n> or all caps how many, and book, snake or radial choose how the wear is laid out across each platform.
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page8.title: demonstrate: more options
trmtgtnh.guide.commands.page8.body: cleararea[=n] clears space first; samearea=x,z pins where it builds; overwrite builds over what is there, replacing only what differs; frozen pins the result; tp moves you to it. warded=h, warded=p or warded=h+p bars mobs from the platforms, and reinforced[=0-3] reinforces them. quick=<n> builds a numbered preset - quick=1+2 or quick=1-6 for several - and quicktp=<n> just takes you to one. tight sets the platforms edge to edge instead of leaving two blocks between them, which reads as one continuous field rather than a grid, and that is easier on the eye when the surfaces are being compared against each other rather than looked at one at a time. realdemo adds the thing a platform cannot show. Behind the exhibit it lays three stretches of road, sixteen blocks by a hundred and twenty-eight - turf, sand, gravel and stone in turn, carrying a rut that is deepest where the feet go and fades to nothing at the verge - because whether a road reads as a road only shows over a distance, and realdemo=<w>x<l> asks for another size. It also stands a row of pens beyond the last platform, one for each golem upgrade the pack allows, each with a golem in it carrying a Wayfarer and chests of tools and material, so the whole crew can be watched working side by side with only the part fitted differing between them. nogolems leaves the pens out; so does switching golems off in the config, in which case they are skipped however the command is typed.
item.trmtgtnh.guide_golem: Wayfarer's Guide: The Golem of Ways
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.title: The Golem of Ways
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.blurb: Building, feeding and upgrading the keeper of paths.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page1.title: A keeper of paths
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page1.body: The Golem of Ways is an earthen figure that maintains ground for you. Give it a radius, tell it what each kind of block should look like, hand it tools and material, and it walks its round keeping every square at the level you asked for - wearing in what is too fresh and mending what is too far gone.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page2.title: Building one
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page2.body: Built where it will stand, like an iron golem. A block of quadruple compressed dirt on the ground, quadruple compressed cobble on top of it, triple compressed dirt as arms either side of the upper block, and any player head placed last to bring it to life. Where those compressed blocks are not available the same shape is built from the plain materials instead.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page3.title: Its screen
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page3.body: Sneak and right-click it. From there you set the radius it works, four blocks to a press, and the point it works around - which starts where you built it. A golem is built at sixteen already, and sixteen is as far as it reaches until the Far Ways upgrade is fitted, so the number on the screen will not climb past it before then however often the button is pressed. Press on anyway if you mean to: what you asked for is remembered even while it cannot be honoured, and fitting the upgrade later opens the round out to it, as far as sixty-four. Each family gets the level of wear you want held, anywhere from pristine to fully worn, or is left alone entirely. To single out one block within a family, hold a stack of it and use the bottom row: that block then follows its own order and ignores its family's, so cobble can be a road while the rest of the stone family stays untouched. WAILA shows who built it and who last changed its orders.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page4.title: Tools and material
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page4.body: Sixteen slots that take two things when you put something in: the tampers it works with, and the ground it mends with - any block from a family the mod wears. Nothing else goes in, though you may take anything out. A hopper or a dropper can top it up as well, but only with the ground it mends with - never a tamper, never an upgrade, and never into its last empty slot, which it keeps free for a tamper to replace one that breaks and for what its work turns up - and no hopper or hopper minecart can take anything out of it. That keeps the tool it depends on and the part it is wearing where you put them, and it means no hopper empties what it gathers: that waits for you, or, with Settled Ways, for the golem to put its surplus away itself. It carries the best tamper it holds, in its hand, where you can see which one it is; it uses that one the way you would and wears it down the same, so it needs restocking. The way you would is meant exactly: a plain tamper moves one square a stroke, because a plain tamper moves one square a click, and a chunk or magic tamper works its whole area at whatever reach you set it to before you handed it over - for the same single use of the tool, and only ever one layer deep, since a golem keeps a surface and not a hole. The reach you leave on a chunk tamper is the difference between a golem that keeps a path and one that keeps a plaza. Its own working turns up seeds, flint and snowballs, and it keeps those in the same store for you to collect - you cannot hand them back once you have taken them, which is why the two rules differ. It leaves what a fight drops where it falls.|There is one thing it takes that its slots will not hold, though: reinforcing material, thrown down where it is working. Whatever reinforce.materials names counts - a bucket of concrete on a pack that has one, obsidian on a world that has not, the same list your own tamper is paid from - and it eats what its round carries it past. It has no eye for a dropped item and will not go and fetch one, so throw it into the ground it keeps rather than across the field. One at a time, and only while its mouth is empty: a bucket goes in, it chews, and the empty comes straight back out at its feet the moment that bucket is finished, so a heap thrown down is eaten steadily rather than vanishing at a stroke. Sixteen mouthfuls is as much as it will hold at once. What it has chewed through is not storage - it does not show on its screen and cannot be taken back out - it is spent instead, one square of its round taken up a level of reinforcement for each mouthful, chosen at random across the whole round rather than stacked three deep at its feet, so a fed golem hardens a road instead of a doorstep.|Two things follow from the bucket coming back that early, and both are deliberate. It will not take a bite at all unless a square of its round is waiting to be reinforced, because by then the container has gone and what is left inside it is material nobody could be handed - so a bucket simply lies there until the ground gives it something to do, and it waits a little before looking again rather than asking every tick. And if it is killed, whatever came in a container is square with you already, while anything that came as a plain block is still owed and falls with the rest. Laying is a stroke of its work like any other, so it needs orders and a tamper in its storage before it will eat at all, and it is the one job that takes nothing off that tamper. Whether it does any of this is a setting, and so is whether it picks anything up: with its picking up switched off it ignores what is thrown down as well, and reinforcing goes back to being a thing done by hand.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page5.title: What it costs
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page5.body: With no tool it does nothing at all. With a tool but no material it can only wear ground down, never mend it. With both it works in either direction.|Mending costs it twice what the same work costs you with a plain or a chunk tamper, as it comes. A plain tamper puts back one step a stroke, and the golem pays two blocks for it where your own single-square mend costs one. A chunk tamper or the Wayfarer's is priced the chunk tamper's way, by the step and for each kind of ground on its own, and the golem pays two blocks wherever a chunk tamper in your hand would pay one. Every stroke is rounded up on its own, though, so a stroke that finds only a step or two of some ground still pays the whole two blocks, and ground it keeps up a step at a time costs it about what a plain tamper would. That is the price of not doing it yourself, and the Frugal upgrade brings it back to parity. It pays even where you would not - with the Wayfarer's Tamper, which costs you nothing, or on a server that has made the chunk tamper free - because a keeper that cost nothing to run would never need looking after.|It also leaves alone any square with something standing on it - a slab, a stair, a carpet, a chest - because wear is drawn on the top face, and ground under a floor shows nothing at all for the tool and the blocks it would cost. Grass, flowers, rails, shallow water and a dusting of snow do not count as standing on it: you can see the ground through those, so it works them as it always did. Whether it knocks the plants flat as it wears a square in is the trampling category's business rather than the golem's: it obeys trampling.groundCover as a walker's worn ground does. The tallies trampling.vegetation and trampling.leaves keep are counted by what walks through or over them, and never by the golem: on a lead or loose, its walking never counts.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page5.body.flat: With no tool it does nothing at all. With a tool but no material it can only wear ground down, never mend it. With both it works in either direction.|Mending costs it two blocks for every step it puts back, whatever tamper it holds: twice what your own single-square mend costs, and up to eight times what a chunk tamper costs you over the same ground, because the chunk tamper rounds a whole area of one kind of ground together and a golem pays for every step on its own. That is the price of not doing it yourself, and the Frugal upgrade halves it. It pays even where you would not - with the Wayfarer's Tamper, or on a server that has made the chunk tamper free - because a keeper that cost nothing to run would never need looking after.|It also leaves alone any square with something standing on it - a slab, a stair, a carpet, a chest - because wear is drawn on the top face, and ground under a floor shows nothing at all for the tool and the blocks it would cost. Grass, flowers, rails, shallow water and a dusting of snow do not count as standing on it: you can see the ground through those, so it works them as it always did. Whether it knocks the plants flat as it wears a square in is the trampling category's business rather than the golem's: it obeys trampling.groundCover as a walker's worn ground does. The tallies trampling.vegetation and trampling.leaves keep are counted by what walks through or over them, and never by the golem: on a lead or loose, its walking never counts.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page6.title: Upgrades
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page6.body: One slot, one upgrade at a time, and each changes both what it does and what it looks like. Range works further out. Speed works faster. Sparing halves the wear on its tools. Frugal halves the blocks it spends. Deep gives it four times the storage - and taking that one back out narrows it again, so anything that will not fit the smaller storage is packed in where there is room, handed to you if you have its screen open, and dropped at its feet if neither. It will never simply keep hold of something it cannot show you. Green turns the level you set into the middle of a band rather than a place to stop, so its round breathes: it wears the whole of its ground down to one edge of that band, turns when it finds nothing left to do, mends it all back up to the other, and goes round again. How wide the band is, is config. Each time a square physically drops a level something may come loose from it - seeds from turf, flint from gravel - and that goes into the golem's own store rather than onto the floor, which is what makes it a farm rather than a mess. Every step back up is paid for at the usual price, as What it costs sets out. Stout doubles its health, and is the only upgrade that gives any of it back - a point an in-game day, which is slow enough that a golem worth looking after stays worth looking after. Fierce doubles what one of its blows takes off. Settled lets it work out of the containers around it rather than only out of itself, which is the one upgrade that changes what the golem is rather than how well it does something.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page7.title: The Golem of All Ways
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page7.body: The upgrade in its slot renames it: of Far Ways, of Swift Ways, of Sparing Ways, of Frugal Ways, of Deep Ways, of Green Ways, of Stout Ways, of Fierce Ways, of Settled Ways. The one past all of those is the hardest thing in the mod to make and carries every one of the nine at once - though not in one step, because nine parts fill a crafting grid and leave nowhere for the nether star. They bind first into an unstable version that carries the whole set and keeps only three to nine of them at a time, choosing again every minute, wearing a corrupted livery and a name it cannot hold still; the star settles that into the real thing. The storage is always among the ones it keeps, so nothing it is carrying is ever stranded by the roll. The settled one earns the only name in the mod that is a pun - the Golem of All Ways. Every golem carries its fitted color in its eyes and in the waystone set in its face, and those stay lit after dark, so you can tell one across a field at night and tell which one. The All Ways golem does not settle on a color at all: its plates, its sigil and its cairn stone turn through the whole set.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page8.title: Standing its ground
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page8.body: A golem with a tamper in its storage will defend the ground it keeps. It hits back at whatever hits it, and it steps in front of a player or a villager a monster has gone for - monsters only, and never a creeper, which it would only blow up its own road over. It does not go hunting; those are the whole of its reasons. A blow costs the tamper a use, exactly as a stroke of work does, so a golem left to fight spends the tools you gave it to work with. Without a tamper it does the opposite and walks away - from creepers too - which is the same emptiness that stops it working. It will stand a little past its radius to reach a fight - or sixteen blocks from home, whichever is further, so a golem told to keep one square is not nailed to it - and no further: a monster that leads it over that line is let go, and the golem walks back to its anchor. Running is the one thing that may take it further, and it comes home afterwards. Two of the upgrades are about this and nothing else: a stout golem has twice the health to spend standing there and mends a point of it a day, and a fierce one takes twice as much off with each blow - though it still needs a tamper in its storage to throw one at all, and still spends that tamper doing it.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page9.title: Working out of a store
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page9.body: The settled upgrade is the only one that reaches outside the golem. With it fitted, a golem that has run out asks the containers around its anchor: a tamper when it has no tool left, a stack of something the ground will take when it has nothing to mend with. What counts as payment is what bone meal and the chunk tamper accept - a block of the ground itself, anything its family lists in its place, or any block of that family where that is allowed - so it can never spend something those would refuse. Your hand tamper goes by a different rule and wants exactly what the ground drops, so a golem mends stone with stone where your tamper wants cobble. When its own storage is full it puts the surplus back - keeping one stack of each thing, so it does not tidy away the very material it is about to spend - and it will only ever put something into a container that is already holding that same thing. It is not a sorting system and must not become one: anything nothing nearby already keeps, it goes on carrying. It reaches into whatever a hopper could reach into, which is chests, barrels, drawers and the rest without any of them being named anywhere, and it reaches its own round plus a little further. Both the switch and that little further are config.
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page10.title: Turning it off
trmtgtnh.guide.golem.page10.body: The golem can be switched off entirely, and so can its upgrades - with those off the slot does not appear at all. Whether it picks up what it finds is its own setting too, whether a settled one may reach into your containers is another, and so is whether it fights at all. All of them are on by default.

trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.flat.line: Every crossing costs the same: for dressed stone
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.flat.detail: Stone does not pack down: a scuff is a scuff, and the hundredth costs what the first did.
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.sod.line: Tears at a touch, then the earth holds: for turf
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.sod.detail: Why a shortcut across a lawn shows before anything else, and the earth beneath gives up far less easily.
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.settle.line: Gives at first, then settles: for sand and gravel
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.settle.detail: Loose grains move under the first passes, then settle into a shape that does not want another.
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.pack.line: Steep at first, then packs hard: for snow
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.pack.detail: One footfall in fresh powder is a whole step; packed snow takes several, and stops getting harder near the end.
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.glaze.line: Dearer every time, twelve times by the end: for ice
trmtgtnh.option.costCurve.glaze.detail: Scuffing ice only polishes it, so every step is dearer than the one before, right to the end.
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.grass.line: Takes the cover off in patches, showing the face beneath
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.grass.detail: What turf does, and anything with a different underside: podzol, mycelium, mossy stone.
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.crack.line: Dulls and splits open, as fissuring stone
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.crack_lite.l: Grimes and hairlines, never breaking up
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.crack_lite.d: The crack run stopped a little over halfway.
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.smooth.line: Buffs flat toward its own average, shiny underfoot
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.smooth_heavy: Buffs harder, leaving a third of the relief
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.dirt.line: Rubs a growing patch away, as a trodden path
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.dirt.detail: What anything unknown falls back to.
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.dirt_lite.de: Three fifths of the face stays exactly as it was.
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.smooth_crack: Buffs the face flat, then cracks it
Buffs the face flat, then wears a track across it
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.crack_dirt.l: Cracks, then wears a track across the cracks
trmtgtnh.option.wearPattern.crack_dirt.d: Named as the Wear Table names it.

trmtgtnh.setting.client.showErosion.summ: Off shows plain terrain, except ruts deep enough to walk into, which always show.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.settingsScreen.s: Which settings screen opens: this one, or the other one where there is one.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.optionsButton.su: Shows a small button for these settings on the game's Options screen.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.overlayDistanceC: Worn ground further away than this is drawn as plain terrain.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.overlayApplyBudg: How many worn squares are put on screen each tick, so busy ground loads in smoothly.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.perSurfaceTextur: Each block wears its own look
Modded grass, dirt and stone wear in their own colors instead of vanilla's.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.wearGradations.s: How many separate pictures each surface's wear is drawn with, from 16 to 80.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.wearRotations.su: How many wear patterns neighbouring blocks share out, so long paths do not look striped.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.maxWearSprites.s: A ceiling on worn-ground pictures in the texture atlas; lower it to save video memory.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.largerAtlas: Use more video memory for wear
trmtgtnh.setting.client.largerAtlas.summ: Lets worn-ground pictures use a 16384 atlas; turn on only with video memory to spare.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.wearNeverStepsBa: Worn ground never jumps back toward clean when it sinks another pixel.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.wearCarriesWithD: How much a deep rut keeps its worn look as it sinks, rather than looking freshly cut.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.wearCurve.summar: Below 1 paths show quickly and deepen slowly; above 1 they wait, then go all at once.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.sideWearFraction: How worn a block's sides look beside its top: 0 is clean, 1 as worn as the floor.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.grassSideWear.su: The green edge on a worn grass block's sides thins toward bare earth as it wears.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.settleOnWornGrou: Snow and carpet settle into ruts
Snow and carpet on worn ground sink down with it instead of hanging in the air.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.inheritAmbientPa: Worn ground keeps giving off the particles of the block beneath, such as spores.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.inheritEntityCol: Worn ground still does what its block does to you, as a Chisel cloud softens a fall.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.inheritShaderMat: With Angelica shaders, worn ground keeps the shine and look of the block beneath.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.innerLayerTextur: Which texture shows through the gaps of a worn block, such as the lava in lavastone.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.animateInnerLaye: Lava or water showing through a worn block keeps moving, for some memory.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.innerLayerAnimat: The most memory moving liquid inside worn blocks may hold; 0 keeps every layer still.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.innerLayerUpload: A safety limit on how many moving inner layers may be redrawn in one tick.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.seeThroughInnerL: Water inside a worn block can be seen through the gaps in its stone.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.liftLayeredBlock: Stops Chisel's lavastone and waterstone flickering where the stone meets the liquid.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.layeredBlockShel: How far Chisel's layered stone is lifted off its liquid; raise it if far flicker shows.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.mapWearThroughTi: Minimaps that read block colors, such as Xaero's, show worn ground darker.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.desirePathHighli: How strongly JourneyMap paints worn ground in the highlight color; 0 is off.
The color JourneyMap tints worn ground toward when the path highlight is on.
trmtgtnh.setting.client.probeLines.summa: Shows how worn a square is, and the rest of this mod's lines, in The One Probe.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.enabled.summary: Off stops all wear and clears it from view; every path comes back when turned on.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.globalSpeed.sum: One dial for the whole mod: 2 makes paths form and heal twice as fast.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.erosionSpeed.su: How fast ground wears: 2 is twice as fast, 0.5 half, and 8 the original mod's pace.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.maxWearFraction: How far along its wear any surface may go, from 0 to 1; 0.25 stops at a light path.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.physicalDecay.s: Whether worn paths sink so you walk down into them, only look sunk, or stay flat.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.grassWearsThrou: A fully worn grass block goes on into bare earth; off, paths thin but never go bald.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.wearThroughToOt: A worn surface goes on as other materials, as stone breaks into cobble, gravel and earth.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.wearPaceFollows: Wear and healing cost what the ground is made of, not what its worn top looks like.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.sneakSuppresses: Sneaking adds no wear, so you can cross a lawn without leaving a trace.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.retriggerCooldo: A mob that just wore a block must leave it a while before it can wear it again.
Players also wait before wearing the same block again, as mobs do.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.retriggerSecond: How long a block a mover just wore is left alone before that mover can wear it again.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.retriggerBlocks: How far a mover must go from a block it wore before it may wear it again early.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.minY.summary: The lowest Y level where ground is ever worn.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.maxY.summary: The highest Y level where ground is ever worn.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.dimensionListIs: On, ground wears only in the listed dimensions; off, everywhere but them.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.dimensionList.s: Which dimensions wear: only these, or every one but these, as its switch says.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.hideWearUnderBl: A block placed on worn ground hides the wear beneath; breaking it brings it back.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.flattenWearUnde: Ground under a placed block keeps its worn look but fills back to a full block.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.blockBreakGrace: How long a broken block's wear and marks are kept, in case the same block goes back.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.wearDropsEnable: Wearing ground has a small chance to drop a seed from grass, a snowball, or flint.
The chance, from 0 to 1, that a step of wear sheds an item.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.bonemealCostsAB: Mending with bone meal also takes a block of the ground being mended from you.
How far a handful of bone meal can reach when mending worn ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.bonemealMaxStep: Most steps one bone meal mends
The most steps of wear one handful of bone meal can mend on a single square.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperCanWear.s: Left-click with a tamper wears ground in on purpose; off, paths come only from walking.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperCanPin.su: Sneak and right-click with a tamper pins a square against wear and healing.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperCooldownT: The least time between two left-clicks with a tamper on the same square.
Blocks one sneak and left-click mend costs; 0 is free and earns no experience.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperPatchCost: Blocks one right-click patch mend costs, for each kind of ground it mends.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperDurabilit: Scales how many uses a tamper lasts against its grade's own figure.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.tamperGrades.su: The metals tampers can be made from, with each grade's uses and reach.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.chunkTamperDefa: How far a newly made chunk tamper reaches; 2 is a five-block cube.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.chunkTamperMaxR: The furthest a chunk tamper may be set to reach; 7 is a chunk's width.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.chunkTamperMaxS: The most steps of wear one chunk tamper use may mend on each square.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.chunkTamperGrad: How many steps of wear one block of material pays a chunk tamper to mend.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.familyEditorOpe: Only operators may change which blocks and creatures wear, from the magic tamper.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.demoContainer.s: What the demonstrate command fills with items: the first one this pack has.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.achievements.su: Adds this mod's own achievement page.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.updateNotice.su: Who is told, as they join, that a newer version of this mod is out.
trmtgtnh.setting.general.updateNoticeRel: Whether the update notice tells of every release, or only those that change this one.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.enabled.summary: Untouched ground recovers over time, even in chunks nobody has visited.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.healingRate.sum: How fast ground recovers: 2 is twice as fast, 0.5 half as fast.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.wearDecayPerDay: The share of unfinished wear that fades each untouched day; 0 turns it off.
Ground stops healing while nobody is connected to the server.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.repairAnyInFami: Any block of a surface mends it
Any block of the same surface can mend worn ground of that surface.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.xpFromHealing.s: Mending worn ground that cost material earns experience.
Experience for each step of wear mended and paid for, before enchantments.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.mendingEnchantm: Name parts that mark an enchantment as one that repairs a tamper from experience.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.xpBoostEnchantm: Name parts that mark an enchantment as one that gives more experience.
trmtgtnh.setting.healing.xpBoostPerLevel: How much each level of an experience boost adds; 0.25 makes level III pay 1.75 times.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.player.summ: Wear added each time a player steps onto a block; every figure here multiplies it.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.fromVillage: Villagers wear the ground, at the villager figure.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.fromPassive: Animals, golems and other passive mobs wear the ground, at the animal figure.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.fromHostile: Every hostile mob, bosses included, wears the ground at the monster figure.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.fromLeashed: Mobs on a lead wear ground
Any mob you lead on a lead wears the ground, at the lead figure.
Each mob the mob list names wears at its own number instead of its group's.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.mobs.summar: Mobs counted by name, each at its own number; 0 keeps that mob off the ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.mounted.sum: How many times more a ridden mount wears the ground than its rider would.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.leashed.sum: How many times more an animal led on a lead wears the ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.villager.su: How hard a villager's step wears the ground, against a player's 1.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.passive.sum: How hard a passive mob's step wears the ground, against a player's 1.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.hostile.sum: How hard a monster's step wears the ground, against a player's 1.
The share of a step's wear passed to the block ahead, softening a path's leading edge.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.bleedSide.s: The share of a step's wear passed to each block beside it, which gives a path its width.

trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.playersPerC: How many players may wear the ground in one chunk at once, while capped.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.capVillager: Only so many villagers wear the ground in one chunk at a time.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.villagersPe: How many villagers may wear the ground in one chunk at once, while capped.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.capPassiveM: Only so many passive mobs wear the ground in one chunk at a time.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.passivePerC: How many passive mobs may wear the ground in one chunk at once, while capped.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.capHostileM: Only so many monsters wear the ground in one chunk at a time.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.hostilePerC: How many monsters may wear the ground in one chunk at once, while capped.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.capCustom.s: Only so many of the mobs the mob list names wear the ground in one chunk at a time.
trmtgtnh.setting.multipliers.customPerCh: How many mobs the mob list names may wear the ground in one chunk at once, while capped.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundCover.s: Plants come down when the ground under them gives way.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundCoverOn: Wait for the ground to sink
Plants come down only when the ground drops a level, not at every step of wear.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundCoverHo: Saplings and flowers hold their square just short of sinking, instead of breaking.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundCoverOn: Plants on hoed ground are trampled and fall too; off, fields are spared.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundCoverDr: The chance a plant taken down by worn ground still drops its item.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.vegetation.su: A plant breaks once enough crossings go through it; it destroys real blocks.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.vegetationDro: The chance a trampled plant drops what it would drop broken by hand.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.leaves.summar: A leaf walked across breaks after enough crossings; it destroys real blocks.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.leavesDropCha: The chance a trampled leaf drops what a decaying leaf would.
trmtgtnh.setting.trampling.groundWearsAw: Ground worn all the way through is removed, dropping nothing; it is not undone.
trmtgtnh.setting.explosions.explosionWea: Explosions wear the ground they do not destroy, leaving a scuffed ring.
trmtgtnh.setting.explosions.explosionStr: How hard a blast scours the ground at its middle, fading to nothing at the edge.
trmtgtnh.setting.explosions.explosionRea: How far the scouring reaches past the blast's own size, as a multiple of it.
trmtgtnh.setting.explosions.explosionMax: How far from a blast the scouring can ever reach, however big the charge.
A limit on the work one blast may do, so a huge charge cannot stall the server.
trmtgtnh.setting.impacts.fallWear.summar: Something landing hard scuffs the patch of ground it lands on.
trmtgtnh.setting.impacts.fallStrength.su: How hard a landing from the reference height marks the ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.impacts.fallReferenceDi: The fall height the landing strength is measured from; raise it for gentler landings.
trmtgtnh.setting.impacts.fallMinDistance: A landing from less than this height marks nothing.
trmtgtnh.setting.impacts.fallMaxRadius.s: How far a landing's scuff can spread, however far the thing fell.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.autoDetect.sum: Sorts installed blocks into grass, dirt, sand, gravel and stone at startup.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.writeDetectedT: Writes what detection finds into each surface's block list, so you can see it.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.exclude.summar: Blocks that never wear, whatever detection finds; names only, no metadata.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.maxTexturedSur: How many block faces get worn pictures of their own; the rest wear their family's.
Maps draw worn ground darker, and toward the color of what it is wearing into.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.mapWearDarkeni: How much darker a fully worn square is drawn on a map, from 0 to 1.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.groundCoverAut: Finds tall grass, flowers, saplings and similar plants at startup, for trampling.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.groundCoverBlo: Plants that come down when the ground under them gives way.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.groundCoverExc: Blocks never treated as ground cover, whatever detection finds.
trmtgtnh.setting.surfaces.groundCoverHol: Ground cover that holds its square instead of coming off it, such as saplings.
Ground cover that never holds its square, whatever detection finds.
trmtgtnh.setting.performance.maxEntriesP: A cap on the worn spots one chunk keeps, so a save cannot grow without end.
trmtgtnh.setting.performance.movementSam: Ticks between checks of each creature's movement.
trmtgtnh.setting.performance.sweepInterv: Ticks between healing sweeps over the loaded chunks.
trmtgtnh.setting.performance.sweepChunks: How many chunks each healing sweep looks at.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.enabled.summa: Whether the reinforce enchantment, its tamper mode and its blast-proofing exist.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.enchantId.sum: The id the reinforce enchantment registers at; -1 takes the first free one.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.materials.sum: What one reinforcement costs, the first the player carries: an item, or fluid:name.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.maxLevel.summ: How many times one block may be reinforced; the top level is blast-proof.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.ceilingLevel1: The blast a once-reinforced block survives, on its own resistance; TNT is 4.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.ceilingLevel2: The blast a twice-reinforced block survives; a third time makes it blast-proof.
trmtgtnh.setting.reinforce.wearFactor.su: Extra lifetimes of wear each reinforcement level adds; 0 leaves wear as it was.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.enabled.summary: Whether the two draughts do anything, can be brewed and turn up in chests.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.lightness.summa: A Draught of Lightness stops its drinker, and their mount, wearing any ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.lightnessSecond: How long one Draught of Lightness lasts.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.lightnessPotion: The effect id Lightness registers at; -1 takes a free one; pin it on every machine.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.heavyFoot.summa: The Draught of the Heavy Foot multiplies its drinker's wear.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.heavyFootFactor: How many ordinary crossings one heavy-footed crossing counts as.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.heavyFootSecond: How long one Draught of the Heavy Foot lasts.
trmtgtnh.setting.potions.heavyFootPotion: The effect id the Heavy Foot registers at; -1 takes a free one.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.snowCovers.summ: Snow on the ground is trodden away layer by layer before the ground beneath wears.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.snowCoverWear.s: How much walking one layer of snow takes before it is trodden away.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.snowCoverFadeDa: Untouched days for a half-trodden snow layer to fill back in; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.fullSnowDriftsS: Snow eight layers deep shelters the ground under it completely.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.wetHealingEnabl: Lets surfaces set to heal only in rain wait for it; off, none of them waits.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.wetHealSecondsP: Seconds of falling rain or snow it takes to mend one step of wear.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.wetHealingNeeds: Ground must see the sky to count as rained on.
Rain healing needs a rainy biome
Ground in a biome that never has weather does not count as rained on.
trmtgtnh.setting.weather.wetHealingSkips: In the Nether, the End and others with no weather, ground heals the ordinary way.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.enabled.summary: Whether the Golem of Ways can be built, spawned or do any work.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.upgrades.summary: Whether golem upgrades exist; off, the golem's screen has no upgrade slot.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.baseRadius.summar: How far from its anchor a golem works without the range upgrade.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.maxRadius.summary: The furthest a golem can ever be told to work, with every upgrade fitted.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.workReach.summary: How far from where it stands a golem can work a square.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.guardRange.summar: How far past its work radius a golem will stand, chase or wander.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.roamFloor.summary: The least ground a golem moves over, however small its round is set.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.storeReach.summar: How far past its ground a settled golem reaches for a container.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.blockCost.summary: How many blocks a golem spends on each purchase of mending.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.scanCooldown.summ: The least time between two full searches of a golem's ground for work.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.targetMemory.summ: How long a golem keeps its list of work before looking over its whole radius again.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.targetLayers.summ: How many rings of nearby work a golem chooses between; 1 always takes the nearest.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.greenBand.summary: How far either side of its order a Green Ways golem wears and mends the ground.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.combat.summary: A golem with a tamper hits back at monsters that attack it or the people near it.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.attackDamage.summ: What each of a golem's blows takes off, once a second; 0 only shoves.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.stoutHealDays.sum: In-game days a stout golem takes to heal one point of health; 0 for none.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.pickUpDrops.summa: A golem keeps the seeds, flint and snowballs its work shakes loose.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.wearDropChance.su: The chance a golem sheds an item each time a square it works drops a level.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.reinforces.summar: A golem picks up reinforcing material thrown beside it and reinforces its round.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.areaStorage.summa: With Settled Ways, a golem takes from and returns to the containers around it.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.idlePoses.summary: A golem standing about shows why, with a pose for each reason it is idle.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.unstableOmni.summ: The nine upgrades bind into an Unstable All Ways, which a nether star then settles.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.unstablePeriod.su: How long an unstable golem keeps one set of upgrades; 1200 is a minute.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.arms.summary: The blocks that form the golem's two arms: the first one this pack has.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.bodyTop.summary: The packed stone that forms the golem's upper body: the first one this pack has.
trmtgtnh.setting.golem.bodyBottom.summar: The packed earth that forms the golem's lower body: the first one this pack has.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.lootFinds.summary: This mod's tools, books, draughts and golem parts turn up in world-generated chests.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.tamper.summary: How often a plain tamper turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.chunkTamper.summar: How often a chunk tamper turns up in dungeon and stronghold chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.wayfarer.summary: How often the Wayfarer's tamper turns up in its chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.wayfarerCategories: Which kinds of chest the Wayfarer's tamper can turn up in, by the game's own name.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.guideBook.summary: How often the Wayfarer's Guide Mk I turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.guideBookRare.summ: How often each of the Mk II, Commands and Golem guides turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.draughtLightness.s: How often a Draught of Lightness turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.draughtHeavyFoot.s: How often a Draught of the Heavy Foot turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.enchantBook.summar: How often each of the three unlock enchanted books turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.golemEgg.summary: How often a dormant Golem of Ways, the rarest find, turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.golemUpgrade.summa: How often each ordinary golem upgrade turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.loot.golemOmniUpgrade.s: How often the All Ways upgrade turns up in chests; 0 is never.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnward.enabled.summa: Whether the spawn ward enchantment, its tamper mode and its spawn barring exist.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnward.enchantId.sum: The id the spawn ward enchantment registers at; -1 takes the first free one.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnward.cost.summary: How many of the material barring one kind of mob from a block costs; 0 is free.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnward.hostileMateri: What barring monsters from a block costs: the first the player has enough of.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnward.passiveMateri: What barring passive mobs from a block costs: the first the player has enough of.
trmtgtnh.setting.pathlight.enabled.summa: Whether the path light enchantment, its tamper mode and its glow exist.
trmtgtnh.setting.pathlight.enchantId.sum: The id the path light enchantment registers at; -1 takes the first free one.
trmtgtnh.setting.pathlight.level.summary: How brightly a lit path glows, where a torch is 14; it keeps no mob from spawning.
trmtgtnh.setting.pathlight.cost.summary: How many of the material lighting one block costs; 0 is free.
trmtgtnh.setting.pathlight.materials.sum: What lighting a block costs: the first the player has enough of.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.gtnhEnhance: Harder recipes, the compressed-block golem and the quest chapter, for GregTech packs.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.questbook.s: Writes a quest line for this mod for BetterQuesting to pick up.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.questbookNo: Tells an operator once when a world's quest book lacks this mod's chapter.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.trophies.su: Writes this mod's trophies for Amazing Trophies to pick up.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.viaRomanaRo: How worn a square must be for Via Romana to count it as road.
How fast worn squares on a charted road heal, against elsewhere.
trmtgtnh.setting.integration.viaRomanaTr: A fast trip along a charted road wears it as if walked.
How much a fast trip wears each road square, in player steps.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.tamper.summa: Gives every player one plain tamper the next time they join; never a second.
Gives every player one chunk tamper the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.wayfarerTamp: Gives every player the Wayfarer's tamper the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.guideMk1.sum: Gives every player the Wayfarer's Guide Mk I the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.guideMk2.sum: Gives every player the Wayfarer's Guide Mk II the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.guideCommand: Gives every player the Commands guide the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.spawnitems.guideGolem.s: Gives every player the Golem of Ways guide the next time they join; never a second.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.enabled.summary: Off, no block counts as this surface, so none of it wears or is trampled.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.autoDetect.summa: Startup detection sorts installed blocks into this surface; off, only the list counts.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.blocks.summary: The blocks that count as this surface; detection fills it, and you may add your own.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.slabs.summary: Slabs of this material count as this surface, just as whole blocks do.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.stairs.summary: Stairs of this material count as this surface, just as slabs do.
Blocks of this surface that wear far more slowly, such as grass paths.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.resistance.summa: How many times more wear the resistant blocks take before each step.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.repairBlocks.sum: Other blocks that can mend this worn surface, besides a block of itself.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.thresholdMin.sum: The least wear one step can need; each spot draws between this and the most.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.thresholdMax.sum: The most wear one step can need; the random draw keeps path edges ragged.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.costCurve.summar: Whether a path shows quickly and then holds, or costs the same all the way down.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.stages.summary: How many steps of wear show on the surface before the ground starts to sink.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.layersPerDepth.s: How many steps of wear each pixel of sinking is split into.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.maxSinkPixels.su: How far the most worn ground sinks, in sixteenths of a block; 0 only discolors.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.maxWear.summary: How far along its wear this surface may go, from 0 to 1 of the whole.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.wearsThroughTo.s: The surfaces that show, in order, as this one wears through.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.healDaysPerStage: In-game days a step of wear must go untouched before the ground mends it back.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.healsOnlyWhenWet: This surface mends only while rain or snow falls on it; the days still bank up.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.wetRecoverySpeed: How many times faster this surface mends while rain falls on it; 1 is no faster.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.wearPattern.summ: The look its worn pictures are made in: patches, cracks, buffing or a rubbed track.
trmtgtnh.setting.family.wearStrength.sum: How strongly the wear look is drawn, 0 to 1; lower keeps more of the block's own look.
